title: The telemetry that couldn't be reconstructed
intro: Post-flight analysis can rebuild the pilot's stick inputs from recorded elevator deflection — except for one band of the envelope, where the reconstruction returns nonsense. Open the clues.

facts.label: The symptom
facts.value: Below 5° of stick, reconstructed input matches the pilot's recorded commands to within 0.01°. Above 5°, the reconstruction returns a different angle on every run — sometimes 6°, sometimes 9°, from identical recorded data.

facts.label: The recorded channel
facts.value: Elevator deflection δ, logged at 200 Hz, 16-bit, no dropouts. Every sample in the bad band reads exactly 10.00°.

facts.label: The chain
facts.value: Stick angle θ → linkage f(θ) = 2θ → hydraulic ram g(x) = clip(x, ±10°) → deflection δ. The ram's mechanical stop is at 10°.

facts.label: The sensors
facts.value: Calibration certificates current. The deflection sensor was bench-tested at 10.00° and reads 10.00°. No drift, no noise floor issue.

facts.label: The solver
facts.value: Reconstruction inverts the linkage as θ = δ/2 and is exact in the linear band. It was rewritten twice, in two languages, with identical results.

question: What actually failed?
choices: The deflection sensor saturates and under-reports above 10°
Nothing is broken — past 5° of stick the ram is against its stop, so every larger angle produces exactly 10°; the map is no longer injective and the original input is unrecoverable in principle
The reconstruction solver has a numerical instability that needs a better root-finder
The 200 Hz log rate aliases the high-rate stick inputs
debrief: This is the one failure no amount of engineering downstream can fix, because nothing is broken. The composite g(f(θ)) = clip(2θ, ±10) is a perfectly good function; it simply stops being **injective** at θ = 5°. Past the stop, the preimage of 10° is not a value but a set — every angle from 5° upward maps there. The information about which one occurred was never encoded in δ, so no solver, no root-finder and no second language can recover it. Rewriting the solver twice was the tell: identical results from independent implementations means the input, not the code. Notice how the plausible answers fail: a saturating *sensor* would be a calibration defect (and the bench test rules it out), and aliasing would corrupt the linear band too. The horizontal-line test names it exactly — the line δ = 10° meets the curve infinitely often. The design fix is upstream and structural: keep the recorded path strictly monotonic, or log stick angle directly so the invertible quantity is the one you store.
